title: Business Case Studies
head: company
line: Real companies, how they evolved, what protects them and the investor lessons each one teaches.

items.relevance: The ultimate example of capital allocation, long-term ownership, and compounding.
items.evolution: Originally a struggling textile company. Warren Buffett transformed it into an investment holding company through insurance float, acquisitions, and ownership of exceptional businesses.
advantages: Insurance Float: insurance premiums provide capital before claims are paid, creating investable funds
Capital Allocation: Berkshire allocates capital across acquisitions, public investments, and internal businesses
Culture: long-term decision-making, low bureaucracy, and an owner mindset
lessons: Capital allocation is a core management skill.
A great business model can create decades of compounding.
The right incentives matter.

items.relevance: A case study in brand power, ecosystems, and customer loyalty.
items.evolution: Originally focused on personal computers. Expanded into iPhone, services, wearables, and a broader digital ecosystem.
advantages: Brand: Apple created significant emotional loyalty
Ecosystem: products reinforce each other, from iPhone and Mac to iCloud, the App Store, and accessories
Pricing Power: a strong brand allows premium pricing
lessons: A competitive advantage can be intangible.
Customer loyalty creates durability.
Great products can create powerful ecosystems.

items.relevance: An example of long-term thinking, reinvestment, and platform economics.
items.evolution: Started as an online bookstore. Expanded into its marketplace, logistics, AWS, and advertising.
advantages: Scale: large infrastructure creates efficiency
Customer Focus: prioritised convenience, selection, and price
Reinvestment Culture: prioritised future growth over short-term profits
lessons: Low short-term profitability can create long-term value.
Platforms can become stronger as they grow.
Management vision matters.

items.relevance: A study in reinvention: dominant in one era, then rebuilt around cloud and AI in the next.
items.evolution: Originally dominated personal computing through Windows. Later expanded into enterprise software, cloud computing, and AI.
advantages: Enterprise Relationships: deep integration into organisations
Switching Costs: businesses depend on Microsoft systems
Recurring Revenue: subscriptions create predictable cash flow
lessons: Great companies can reinvent themselves.
Adaptability is a competitive advantage.
Strong ecosystems create durability.

items.relevance: A case study in how a simple, aligned business model can become an exceptional investment.
items.evolution: A membership warehouse model in which customers pay annually for access to discounted products.
advantages: Membership Model: creates recurring revenue
Customer Trust: a consistent value proposition
Operational Efficiency: low margins but high customer loyalty
lessons: Simple businesses can be exceptional investments.
Customer trust can become a moat.
Alignment creates loyalty.

items.relevance: A case study in how brand, distribution, and habit can compound for generations.
items.evolution: Built a global beverage brand through distribution, marketing, and brand recognition.
advantages: Brand: one of the strongest consumer brands globally
Distribution Network: global availability
Customer Habit: frequent, repeat consumption
lessons: Brands can last generations.
Distribution is often overlooked.
Boring businesses can compound.

items.relevance: A study in disrupting your own business model before someone else does.
items.evolution: Transformed from DVD rental into a streaming platform, and then into a content producer in its own right.
advantages: Data: uses customer behaviour to improve recommendations
Scale: a global subscriber base
Adaptability: successfully disrupted its own business model
lessons: Great companies adapt before they are forced.
Disruption creates winners and losers.

items.relevance: A case study in separating genuine opportunity from speculation when future expectations dominate a valuation.
items.evolution: Started as an electric vehicle company. Expanded into energy storage, software, and autonomous driving ambitions.
advantages: Brand: strong customer enthusiasm
Manufacturing Innovation: a focus on efficiency and scale
Software Potential: vehicle data creates optionality
lessons: Future expectations heavily influence valuations.
Innovation requires separating opportunity from speculation.

items.relevance: A case study in how infrastructure businesses can capture a major technology trend.
items.evolution: Originally known for graphics processors. Expanded into AI computing, data centres, and a broader software ecosystem.
advantages: Technology Leadership: a strong position in AI chips
Ecosystem: software creates additional value beyond hardware
Market Position: a critical infrastructure provider
lessons: Infrastructure businesses can capture major technology trends.
Growth expectations must still be analysed.

items.relevance: A study in failure, adaptation, and disruption.
items.evolution: Blockbuster dominated physical video rental. Streaming changed the industry. Netflix adapted; Blockbuster failed to transition effectively, weighed down by business model attachment, slow adaptation, and short-term incentive problems.
risks: Business Model Attachment: protected existing revenue
lessons: Past success does not guarantee future success.
Competitive advantages can disappear.
Management adaptability matters.

items.relevance: A case study in network effects, asset-light business models, and infrastructure economics.
items.evolution: Evolved from a credit card network into global payment infrastructure. Visa does not primarily lend money; it facilitates transactions between consumers, merchants, and banks.
advantages: Network Effects: the system becomes more valuable as more consumers and merchants join
Scale: global acceptance creates a powerful advantage
Asset-Light Model: benefits from payment volume without owning traditional banking infrastructure
lessons: The strongest businesses often own the network, not the product.
Infrastructure businesses can quietly compound for decades.

items.relevance: A companion case to Visa in payment network economics.
items.evolution: Transformed from a card network into a global digital payments platform.
advantages: Global Network: millions of businesses and consumers rely on its infrastructure
Trust: payments require reliability, security, and speed
Digital Transition: long-term growth from cash replacement, digital payments, and emerging markets
lessons: Great businesses solve essential problems.
Convenience can become a powerful moat.

items.relevance: A case study in how deep technical complexity itself can be a moat, with no consumer brand required.
items.evolution: Became a critical supplier of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
advantages: Technological Complexity: extreme engineering difficulty creates barriers to entry
Monopoly-Like Position: few companies possess comparable capabilities
Customer Dependence: leading semiconductor manufacturers rely on ASML technology
lessons: Competitive advantages can come from complexity.
A company does not need a consumer brand to possess a powerful moat.

items.relevance: A case study in how deep specialisation and long-term research investment can compound.
items.evolution: Built expertise in diabetes care and later expanded through obesity treatments.
advantages: Scientific Expertise: deep specialised knowledge
Research Capability: long-term investment in innovation
Healthcare Demand: addresses large global health challenges
lessons: Specialisation can create enormous expertise advantages.
Long-term research investment can compound.

items.relevance: A case study in how intangible assets like brand and scarcity create pricing power.
items.evolution: Built a portfolio of premium brands across fashion, jewellery, spirits, and beauty.
advantages: Brand Power: luxury brands create emotional value beyond functionality
Scarcity: maintaining exclusivity protects pricing power
Portfolio Strategy: combines multiple strong brands
lessons: Intangible assets can create enormous economic value.
Pricing power is one of the strongest competitive advantages.

items.relevance: A case study in turning a commodity into a branded experience.
items.evolution: Transformed coffee from a commodity into a branded experience.
advantages: Brand Experience: customers buy convenience, habit, environment, and identity
Store Network: scale creates operational advantages
Customer Data: digital loyalty creates deeper relationships
lessons: Companies can create new categories through positioning.
Customer habits can become economic moats.

items.relevance: A case study in reinventing a business model without reinventing the product.
items.evolution: Transitioned from one-time software purchases to subscription-based recurring revenue.
advantages: Customer Dependence: creative professionals rely on Adobe tools
Recurring Revenue: subscriptions improve predictability
Ecosystem: products reinforce each other
lessons: Great companies can reinvent themselves.
Business model innovation can be as important as product innovation.

items.relevance: A case study in how a historic technology advantage can quietly disappear.
items.evolution: Intel historically dominated computer processors. Competitive advantages weakened due to manufacturing challenges, increased competition, and changing industry dynamics.
lessons: A historic advantage can disappear.
Past dominance does not guarantee future success.
Innovation requires continuous investment.

items.relevance: A case study in mistaking growth and narrative for value creation.
items.evolution: WeWork presented itself as a technology-enabled platform transforming office space. The business struggled because growth exceeded economics, long-term lease obligations created risk, and profitability remained challenging.
lessons: Growth does not equal value creation.
Revenue growth must eventually translate into attractive economics.
Business models matter more than narratives.

items.relevance: A case study in how a company can be excellent at one game and still lose when the game changes.
items.evolution: Nokia became one of the world's dominant mobile phone companies, with huge global market share, strong brand recognition, and an excellent engineering reputation. The smartphone revolution shifted the industry from hardware dominance to software ecosystems and platforms, and competitors with stronger software ecosystems gained ground.
advantages: Historically: huge global market share
Historically: strong brand recognition
Historically: an excellent engineering reputation
risks: Protecting the past rather than building the future
lessons: Competitive advantage is temporary.
Great companies evolve before they are forced to.
The most dangerous sentence in business is: we have always done it this way.

items.relevance: Nokia's companion case: a company that kept adapting around its underlying purpose instead of defending a single product.
items.evolution: Canon's original strength was cameras. It repeatedly expanded its underlying capability into imaging technology, printing, and medical equipment, while maintaining its underlying purpose of helping people capture and reproduce information. The product changed. The capability survived.
advantages: Purpose-Led Adaptation: redefined itself around a durable purpose rather than a single product
Diversified Imaging Expertise: applied core optical and imaging know-how across cameras, printers, and medical equipment
Customer Focus Over Competitor Focus: focused on continuing to serve customers and improve, rather than only on beating rivals
lessons: A company that focuses on its underlying purpose can survive the decline of any single product.
Playing an infinite game, continuing to adapt and improve, differs from playing a finite game focused only on beating competitors.
Diversifying around a core capability can be safer than diversifying around a single product line.
